description: We are the team MindMesh passionate about AI, data analysis, and software development. For the Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we aim to explore NASA’s Earth observation data, identify meaningful environmental trends, and visualize changes across different regions over time. Our goal is to transform complex scientific data into clear, interactive, and accessible insights that help people understand our changing planet. We are excited to combine technology, data-driven analysis, and creative problem-solving to build a meaningful solution.
summary: CaseFile Earth is a free website that lets anyone check whether the climate where they live is really changing, and how sure we can be. Pick any place on Earth (one of 224 countries, a Bangladesh division or any 1° square), or two places to compare, and see its past against its present in NASA data from 1980 to 2025. Ten records are covered: temperature, rain, snowfall, wind, water vapour, air pressure, soil moisture, evaporation, runoff and plant greenness. The site shows each year against a 1991–2020 baseline, each month with the seasons removed, the first ten years against the last ten, and every trend with its 95% range. For the questions we registered before looking at any trend (temperature and rain in Bangladesh and its neighbours), one tested statistics engine gives a graded answer or an honest "can't tell yet", with its evidence. This answers the challenge directly: people become trend detectives themselves and learn that one hot summer is not a trend. It works in English and Bangla, and even offline.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

CaseFile Earth answers one question with care: is the climate where I live really changing, and how sure can we be?

• Any place, any record: turn a 3D globe and click anywhere, or search. Each of 224 countries, the Bangladesh divisions, West Bengal and any 1° square has its own report covering ten NASA records.

• Past against present: "What is changing here" puts every record side by side, with its trend per decade, the change between its first and last ten years, and a stripe per year. "Then and now" shows yearly values with a 10-year average, each year against the 1991–2020 baseline, a year-by-month heatmap with the normal seasonal cycle removed, each month's average in the first and last ten years, the trend of each calendar month, and temperature and rain through the year in both periods.

• The whole planet: the globe plays every year from 1980 to 2025 as values, as differences from the baseline, or as "the last ten years minus the first ten". The Trends screen ranks countries by their tested trend with 95% ranges, maps every country's trend, and shows latitude against year.

• Graded answers to registered questions: for temperature and rain in Bangladesh, its divisions and its neighbours, and for pairs such as Bangladesh against West Bengal, the site gives a graded answer with its evidence, a sensitivity check against NASA's IMERG satellite rainfall, and what could overturn it. When the evidence is not strong enough, it says "can't tell yet" and explains why.

• English and Bangla on every screen. A single offline file keeps working without the internet.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: a Python pipeline finds every NASA file through NASA Earthdata (the CMR catalogue, with the earthaccess library), downloads only the variables it needs, and records each file's SHA-256 fingerprint, so anyone can rebuild the results.

2. Places: country and region outlines (Natural Earth, geoBoundaries) become area-weighted grid cells on each dataset's own grid.

3. Pre-registration: before any real trend was computed, the team committed which places, records, seasons and thresholds would be tested. The build refuses to run a test that was not registered.

4. One tested engine: every statistic comes from one Python engine covered by automated tests. It uses a Mann–Kendall trend test that allows for year-to-year memory in the climate, a Sen slope with its 95% range, false-discovery-rate control across many places, and a change-point flag.

5. A website that computes nothing (React, TypeScript, Observable Plot, globe.gl) only reads the result files and draws them. It computes no statistic. Everything except the optional copilot is static and also works offline.
6. The investigation copilot: an AI model (Google Gemini) can only call fixed tools that read the site's own result files. It chooses which evidence to open and words short answers; it never computes, changes or decides a number or verdict, and every number it writes is checked against the result files before it is shown.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

• People in Bangladesh, and anywhere else, get an honest, checkable answer instead of an impression from one hot summer or one flood.

• Students and teachers get a hands-on way to learn what a trend is, how uncertain it is, and why "can't tell yet" is not "no change".

• Journalists and local planners can compare places and records quickly, with the evidence and the data sources on every screen.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most climate tools show a chart and stop there. CaseFile Earth treats every claim like a case file: what changed, how sure we are, and what could overturn it. Questions are registered before the data are seen. "Can't tell yet" is treated as a real, honest answer. Every number traces back to a fingerprinted NASA file.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Model output is labelled as model output (MERRA-2 is a reanalysis). IMERG satellite rainfall is used as a sensitivity check, never as a confirmation. Careful wording ("consistent with", never "caused by"). Accessibility, Bangla for local users, and offline use where the internet is weak.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, h5py, netCDF4, shapely, earthaccess; tests with pytest). TypeScript and React with Vite, Tailwind CSS, Observable Plot and globe.gl / three.js (tests with Vitest and Playwright). Hosted on Vercel (with the copilot) and GitHub Pages (without it), checked with GitHub Actions. Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/asifff113/NasaEarthDetective

USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code, with Anthropic's Claude models) to help write the specification, the statistics engine, the data pipeline, the website and the English and Bangla interface text. Automated tests and our team checked the results. The team made the design, method, threshold and region decisions, and registered them before looking at any trend. Every number comes from our tested Python engine. The site has one optional AI feature, the investigation copilot (Google Gemini): it chooses evidence and words, never computes or decides a number or verdict, and every number it shows is checked against the result files. Videos: the screens are recordings of our real website; the narration is an AI-generated voice (Microsoft Edge neural text-to-speech), stated on screen, in the video descriptions and in the file metadata; the cards, captions and editing were made by scripts written with an AI coding assistant. No AI image or video generation was used, and no NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
VIDEO TOUR: an 8-minute narrated tour of the whole site, with chapters: https://youtu.be/e0cjM7Ls0KI (also on the site's "Watch a case" page).

Team CaseFile Earth: Asif Istiaque (AI researcher, team leader), Hirok Reza (backend developer), Shakil Khan (frontend developer).
